title: Sort by swapping
intro: `Arrays.sort` puts an array's values in ascending order, smallest first. Do its job by hand: click two boxes to swap them, until no value is bigger than the one after it.

rounds.prompt: Sort `{name}` into ascending order: click two boxes to swap them.

why.wasted: Neither value landed in its final place. Find the smallest value that isn't home yet: it belongs in the lowest box that isn't sorted.

rounds.prompt: Six values this time, some below zero. Sort `{name}` into ascending order.
rounds.right: Sorted in {verdict} The negative values come first: ascending means smallest first.

why.wasted: Neither value landed in its final place. A negative number is smaller than 0, so the most negative value goes in box 0.

rounds.prompt: `b = a`, then `b` is sorted. Has `a` changed?
rounds.right: One array, two names: `b = a` copies the arrow, not the boxes, so sorting through `b` sorts what `a` sees too.

why.sortChangesA: `int[] b = a;` copies the arrow, not the boxes: `a` and `b` point at one array. Sorting it through `b` sorts the only array there is.

rounds.prompt: This time `b` is a copy of `a`, and then `b` is sorted. Has `a` changed?
rounds.aside: `b` is a copy of `a`: new boxes, holding the same values. (Making a copy like this is up to you in DIY 5.)
rounds.right: Two arrays: sorting the copy rearranges its own boxes and leaves the original exactly as it was.

why.sortChangesA: `b` points at its own boxes. `Arrays.sort(b)` rearranges those, and `a`'s array is a different object, so it keeps its order.
